narrative.overview: Tessera is an instrument for watching an agent work, so the interface borrows the material of a working notebook: warm paper, ink, a hairline rule between entries, and one vermilion signal that appears only when something happens. Every region answers a question the operator would ask mid-demo: where am I, what did the agent do, is it alive. The mood is quiet, precise, slightly archival; it must not read as a generic AI dashboard. The category-interchangeable test is the gate: remove the Vietnamese copy and the screenshot should still read as a console for observing an agent's tool calls. The ink status bar, the grotesk display voice, the mono readouts and the stacked architecture page keep it specific. Both themes are first-class and every token has a dark counterpart.
keyCharacteristics: Warm paper + ink surfaces, hairline borders doing all the structural work; no gradients, no glass.
One vermilion signal accent; success/warning/danger appear only as small status marks.
Be Vietnam Pro for display, Be Vietnam Pro for UI, Roboto Mono for machine data.
Flat surfaces at rest; shadow only answers how far off the page something is.
Dense, readable readouts: tabular numerals, uppercase micro-labels, an ink status strip.

rules.name: The One Signal Rule
rules.body: Signal Vermilion covers at most ~10% of any screen: one primary button, one active nav item, one user bubble side, key figures. Its rarity is what makes it read as signal.

rules.name: The Two-Theme Parity Rule
rules.body: Every colour used in a component resolves through a token with a dark counterpart. A raw hex inside a component is a defect.

rules.name: The Machine Data Rule
rules.body: Monospace is a signal, not a costume: if a human would read it aloud as a sentence, it is Be Vietnam Pro. Figures use tabular numerals so a KPI never jitters as it updates.

rules.name: The Border Does the Work Rule
rules.body: If a surface needs to be distinguished, give it a hairline before giving it a shadow. Shadows may only answer how far off the page something is, never what it is.

rules.name: The 12 px Floor Rule
rules.body: Functional micro-text — labels, meta rows, keyboard hints, badges — never goes below 0.75 rem. It sits on tinted and paper surfaces, so a smaller size fails legibility long before it fails contrast.

rules.name: The No-Gradient Rule
rules.body: No gradient, no backdrop-filter, no dot-grid, no decorative texture. The only depth cue is a hairline; the only colour event is the signal.

rules.name: The Display Restraint Rule
rules.body: Serif is for page titles and the two architecture headings only. Tool names, KPI figures and buttons stay in Plex Sans; a serif on a control would read as decoration.

dos: Do express every colour through a token; if a value is needed in a component, add the token first (light + dark pair).
Do let the 1px hairline carry structure, then add the rest or lift shadow step.
Do keep Signal Vermilion for action and state, and keep it under ~10% of the screen.
Do set numbers in tabular figures and machine strings in Roboto Mono.
Do use sentence case for headings and titles, with -0.02em tracking on display only.
Do keep the status bar inside the first viewport (100dvh - header - status bar).
Do give destructive actions an in-place confirm step rather than acting on first click.
Do honour prefers-reduced-motion; motion is 140-220ms and decorative only.
donts: Don't bring back the base library's hard 8px offset shadows or 0px radius — that look is the anti-reference.
Don't uppercase a page heading (dqcss's default h1 transform is overridden on purpose).
Don't introduce a second accent hue; success/warning/danger are status marks, not decoration.
Don't use monospace for sentences, labels, or buttons.
Don't put a gradient, blur or dot-grid anywhere. The brand mark is flat ink.
Don't stack two shadow steps on the same surface, or use shadow to signal hover.
Don't hard-code #fff/#000 in components; use Surface / On Accent / Ink.
Don't build page structure from equal-sized card grids; give the page one entry point.
